<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{intro:main-orientation-theorem}
Let $X$ be a smooth complex algebraic Calabi--Yau fourfold, not necessarily
proper, with a chosen trivialization of $K_X$. Write
$\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}$ for the derived moduli stack of perfect complexes
with compact support, and $O^\omega_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}$ for its
orientation $\mathbb Z_2$-bundle. Suppose that
\begin{equation}\label{intro:steenrod-condition}
 \int_X\bar\alpha\smile\operatorname{Sq}_c^2(\bar\alpha)=0
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z_2
 \quad\text{for every }\alpha\in H_c^3(X;\mathbb Z),
\end{equation}
where $\bar\alpha$ is reduction modulo $2$ and
$\operatorname{Sq}_c^2$ is the Steenrod square on cohomology with compact
support. Then:

\begin{enumerate}
\item The bundle $O^\omega_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}$ is trivializable.
A flag structure on $X$ natural at zero, understood with compact supports
when $X$ is noncompact, determines such a trivialization. For the definition of flag structures, see \S\ref{sec:canonical-orientations-and-flag-structures}.
\item For $\xi\in K_c^0(X)$, let $\mathcal M_{X,\xi}^{\rm cs}$ be the
substack on which the compactly supported topological $K$-theory class is $\xi$.
If
\begin{equation}\label{intro:kappa-condition}
 \kappa(\xi):=c_2(\xi)-c_1(\xi)^2=0
 \quad\text{in }H_c^4(X;\mathbb Z),
\end{equation}
then the induced orientation on $\mathcal M_{X,\xi}^{\rm cs}$ is
independent of the flag-structure natural at zero. It is therefore
canonical. These canonical orientations are compatible with excision
under open embeddings preserving the Calabi--Yau structures, whenever
the theorem applies to both source and target.
\end{enumerate}
The same conclusions hold for a complex analytic Calabi--Yau fourfold
and its moduli stack of analytic perfect complexes with compact support.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{intro:local-theorem}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $Y$ be a smooth complex algebraic threefold and
$p:X=\operatorname{Tot}_Y(K_Y)\to Y$. There is a canonical orientation
$o_{\rm Shi}$ on $\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}$. More precisely, for the
universal complex $\mathcal E$, put
$\mathcal G=\mathbf R(\operatorname{id}\times p)_*\mathcal E$ and
$\mathcal V=\mathbf R\pi_*\mathbf R\mathcal Hom(\mathcal G,\mathcal G)$,
where $\pi:\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}\times Y\to\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}$.
The orientation is given by the canonical trivialization
\[
 K_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}
 \cong\det\mathcal V\otimes(\det\mathcal V)^\vee
 \cong\mathcal O_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}.
\]

The analogous
trivialization defines $o_{\rm Shi}$ on the topological $K$-theory space which we denote by 
$\mathcal C_{X}^{\rm cs}$.

\item Let $N$ be an almost  complex manifold of real dimension six,
let $K_N=\det_{\mathbb C}(T_N)^\vee$, and consider the Thom pair
$(Z_N,\partial Z_N)=(D(K_N),S(K_N))$ of the disc bundle and the corresponding sphere bundle. 

For
$\beta\in K^0(N)$, set
$\xi=\operatorname{Th}^{KU}_{K_N}(\beta)\in K^0(Z_N,\partial Z_N)$.
The topological version of \eqref{intro:steenrod-condition} holds on
$(Z_N,\partial Z_N)$. Moreover, if
$c_2(\xi)-c_1(\xi)^2=0$ in $H^4(Z_N,\partial Z_N;\mathbb Z)$, then
\[
 o_{\rm Shi}|_\xi=o_{\rm JU}|_\xi,
\]
where $o_{\rm JU}$ is the canonical orientation obtained from the
relative bordism construction. 

\item Let $C$ be a compact Riemann surface and $E\to C$ a holomorphic
vector bundle of rank three with an isomorphism $\det E\cong K_C$.
On the compactly-supported $K$-theory space $X=\operatorname{Tot}_C(E)$, both orientations are well-defined everywhere and agree.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{intro:PT-family-theorem}
(a) Let $\pi:\mathfrak X\to B$ be a smooth, topologically locally trivial
complex analytic family of fourfolds with a relative Calabi--Yau
structure. Let $\mathcal P=\mathcal P(\mathfrak X/B)$ be the relative
stack of stable pairs $s:\mathcal O_{X_b}\to\mathcal F$, where
$\mathcal F$ is pure of dimension one with proper support and
$\operatorname{coker}s$ has support of dimension at most zero. Then
$O^\omega_{\mathcal P}$ has a canonical trivialization compatible with
base change. 

(b) On each fibre admitting a flag structure natural at zero,
this trivialization agrees with the induced Joyce--Upmeier orientation.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Let us also mention that \cite{Bojko2021} was written before Joyce and Upmeier modified their
erroneous argument in \cite{CaoGrossJoyce2020} to the one in \cite{JU}.
Once this modification was made, Bojko’s original argument for orientability (which was originally
dependent on \cite{CaoGrossJoyce2020}), on the nose, stopped working whenever $H_3^c (X)\neq 0$, that is, under
conditions somewhat weaker than the condition (1.1).

However, after the first author of the present work discussed with A. B. some ideas used
below, Bojko was able to introduce minor changes which now make his train of thought work
for all quasi-projective Calabi-Yau $4$-folds satisfying (1.1).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{H4rem}
\begin{enumerate}
\item The comparison map $\Gamma_X$ is canonical up to homotopy, but not in
general up to a unique homotopy; compare
\cite[Section 2]{JoyceTanakaUpmeier2020}.  This ambiguity is immaterial for
the constructions below, as in \cite[2.3.5]{JoyceTanakaUpmeier2020}.
\item The same construction applies to other representing spaces.  In
particular, for a smooth topologically locally trivial family
$\mathfrak X\to U$ one may form the relative space
$\mathcal H^4_{\rm cs}(\mathfrak X/U)$ whose fiber over $u\in U$ is
\[
\operatorname{Map}_*(\mathfrak X_u^+,K(\mathbb Z,4)).
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
The algebraic and topological orientation bundles
$O^{\omega}_{\mathcal M_X}\to\mathcal M_X$ and
$O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_X}\to\mathcal C_X$ are the principal
$\mathbb Z_2$-bundles whose fibers consist of square roots of
$Q_{\mathcal M_X}$ and $Q_{\mathcal C_X}$, respectively.  Equivalently, the
fiber over a point is the set of isomorphisms $\phi:K\xrightarrow{\cong}
\mathbb C$ for which
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
K^{\otimes2}\arrow[r,"Q"]\arrow[d,"\phi^{\otimes2}"']&\mathbb C
\arrow[d,"\mathrm{id}"]\\
\mathbb C^{\otimes2}\arrow[r,"m"']&\mathbb C
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commutes.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
All the material in this subsection has a natural relative version for
relatively Calabi--Yau, topologically locally trivial families, whose fibers
may be non-compact, as in Subsection~\ref{stacks}.  For example, the topological
determinant line is classified by the composite
\[
\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}
\xrightarrow{\pi_!^{KU,\mathbb C}}U\times KU
\xrightarrow{\operatorname{pr}_2}KU\xrightarrow{\det}B\mathbb C^*.
\]
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{origJU}
There is a canonical isomorphism of principal $\mathbb Z_2$-bundles
\[
I_X:\Gamma_X^*O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_X}
\xrightarrow{\cong}O^{\omega}_{\mathcal M_X},
\]
compatible with direct sums.  It is induced by the canonically
homotopy-commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\mathcal M_X^{\rm top}\arrow[r,"\Gamma_X"]
 \arrow[d,"\pi_*^{\rm alg}"']&
\mathcal C_X\arrow[d,"\pi_!^{KU,\mathbb C}"]\\
\operatorname{Perf}(\mathbb C)^{\rm top}
 \arrow[dr,"\det"']&KU\arrow[d,"\det"]\\
&B\mathbb C^* ,
\end{tikzcd}
\]
and this diagram is compatible with the Serre-duality quadratic forms.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
 Joyce and Upmeier define $O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_X}$ analytically, using
families of twisted Dirac operators.  However, the families Atiyah--Singer index theorem
identifies their construction with the topological $K$-theoretic construction
above. 


\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{compfamc}
Let $\pi:\mathfrak X\to U$ be a smooth proper family of complex varieties of
complex dimension $4n$, equipped with a relative Calabi--Yau structure.
Suppose that all fibers are projective and the total space is quasi-projective.
Then there is a canonical isomorphism
\[
I_{\mathfrak X/U}:
\Gamma_{\mathfrak X/U}^*O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}}
\xrightarrow{\cong}O^{\omega}_{\mathcal M_{\mathfrak X/U}}.
\]
It is induced by the homotopy-commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\mathcal M_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm top}
 \arrow[r,"\Gamma_{\mathfrak X/U}"]
 \arrow[d,"\pi_*^{\rm alg}"']&
\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}\arrow[d,"\pi_!^{KU,\mathbb C}"]\\
U\times\operatorname{Perf}(\mathbb C)^{\rm top}
 \arrow[d,"\operatorname{pr}_2"']&U\times KU
 \arrow[d,"\operatorname{pr}_2"]\\
\operatorname{Perf}(\mathbb C)^{\rm top}
 \arrow[dr,"\det"']&KU\arrow[d,"\det"]\\
&B\mathbb C^* .
\end{tikzcd}
\]
This diagram is compatible with the relative Serre duality.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:pushforward-without-quasiprojectivity}
Let $f:Z\to W$ be a proper smoothable morphism between smooth proper complex
varieties.  Thus $f$ admits a factorization through a closed immersion followed
by a smooth morphism.  Derived direct image defines an exact functor
$\mathbf Rf_*:\operatorname{Perf}(Z)\to\operatorname{Perf}(W)$ and hence a
map $\mathcal M_Z\to\mathcal M_W$.  Then the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
\mathcal M_Z^{\rm top}
 \arrow[r,"(\mathbf Rf_*)^{\rm top}"]
 \arrow[d,"\Gamma_Z"']&
\mathcal M_W^{\rm top}
 \arrow[d,"\Gamma_W"]\\
\mathcal C_Z\arrow[r,"f_!^{KU,\mathbb C}"']&\mathcal C_W
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commutes up to a natural homotopy, compatibly with composition of proper
smooth morphisms.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{compnc2}
Let $X$ be a smooth quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb C$. Then the
diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
	{(\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs})^{\rm top}} &&
	{\mathcal C_X^{\rm cs}} \\
	{\operatorname{Perf}(\mathbb C)^{\rm top}} && KU \\
	& {B\mathbb C^*}
	\arrow["{\Gamma_X}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\pi_*^{\rm alg}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\pi_!^{KU,\mathbb C}}", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\det}"', from=2-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow["{\det}", from=2-3, to=3-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
canonically commutes.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
\textbf{Step 0.} The proof is similar to the argument of \cite{BFM}. The main
statement of that paper implies that, if $X$ is a smooth projective variety, the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
	{K^{\rm alg}(X)} & {K^{\rm top}(X)} \\
	{K^{\rm alg}(\operatorname{pt})} &
	{K^{\rm top}(\operatorname{pt})}
	\arrow["{\Gamma_X}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\pi_{X*}^{\rm alg}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\pi_{X!}^{KU,\mathbb C}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\Gamma_{\operatorname{pt}}}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commutes.

Thus there are, as one can see, two main differences from our context:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item In their proof, the authors work not with $K$-theory but with
    so-called \textit{$K$-homology}, which, however, coincides with $K$-theory
    for smooth varieties. They also work at the level of $K$-groups, rather
    than their categorification, that is, rather than at the level of mapping
    stacks.
    \item They do not consider the compactly supported variant of the theory.
\end{enumerate}

However, inspecting the proof in \cite{BFM}, one sees that these differences
do not affect the argument, and the proof generalizes verbatim.

\textbf{Step 1.} For the convenience of the reader, we sketch the argument.
First, embed $X$ into $\mathbb P^n$ via an embedding
$\iota:X\to\mathbb P^n$, and prove that the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}\label{BFMdiag}
	{(\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs})^{\rm top}} &
	{\mathcal M_{\mathbb P^n}^{\rm top}} \\
	{\mathcal C_X^{\rm cs}} & {\mathcal C_{\mathbb P^n}}
	\arrow["{\iota_*^{\rm alg}}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\Gamma_X}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\Gamma_{\mathbb P^n}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
		\arrow["{\iota_!^{KU,\mathbb C}}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commutes, as in \cite[Sections 2, 4]{BFM}.

\textbf{Step 2.} Then observe the factorization of the morphism
$X\to\operatorname{pt}$ as
\[
X\xrightarrow{\iota}\mathbb P^n\longrightarrow\operatorname{pt},
\]
and, to deal with the second arrow, apply Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-without-quasiprojectivity} to the smooth
variety $\mathbb P^n$.

The fact that the whole procedure is independent of the choice of the
embedding $\iota$ is proved as in \cite[Sections 2, 4]{BFM}, using deformation
to the normal cone.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
Let $\pi:\mathfrak X\to U$ be a smooth but non-proper algebraic family which
is known to be topologically locally trivial. Then there is a natural
commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}\label{diagfam2}
	{(\mathcal M_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs})^{\rm top}} &&
	{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}} \\
	{U\times\operatorname{Perf}(\mathbb C)^{\rm top}} && {U\times KU} \\
	& {B\mathbb C^*.}
	\arrow["{\Gamma_{\mathfrak X/U}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\pi_*^{\rm alg}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\pi_!^{KU,\mathbb C}}", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\det\circ\operatorname{pr}_2}"', from=2-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow["{\det\circ\operatorname{pr}_2}", from=2-3, to=3-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
One argues similarly to what was done above.

First, note that any family $\mathfrak X\to U$ as in the theorem admits a
description as the composition of a locally closed embedding
$\mathfrak X\to\mathfrak Y$ into a family of smooth projective varieties over
the base and the projection $\mathfrak Y\to U$.

Indeed, choose a smooth compactification $\mathfrak J$ of the total space of
$\mathfrak X$, and embed $\mathfrak X$ into $\mathfrak J\times U$ via the
graph map.

Since $\mathfrak X\to\mathfrak Y$ is fiberwise a locally closed embedding of
smooth varieties, one proves that the algebraic and topological pushforwards
canonically coincide. This is analogous to diagram~\ref{BFMdiag}.

The step $\mathfrak Y\to U$ is, by now, clear: one uses Proposition \ref{prop:pushforward-without-quasiprojectivity} in families.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
Let $\pi:\mathfrak X\to U$ be a relatively Calabi--Yau, not necessarily
proper, topologically locally trivial family of complex $4n$-folds over an
algebraic space $U$.

We use below the spin structure determined by the relative Calabi--Yau
structure.

Define the real determinant line bundle
$L^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}}$ by the classifying map
\[
\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}
\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Ad}_{\mathfrak X/U}}
\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\mathbb R,\rm cs}
\xrightarrow{\pi_!^{KO}}
U\times KO
\xrightarrow{\operatorname{pr}_2}
KO
\xrightarrow{\det_{\mathbb R}}
\mathbb RP^\infty.
\]
Here $\operatorname{Ad}_{\mathfrak X/U}$ is the Joyce--Upmeier adjoint-class
map. Denote by
\[
O\bigl(L^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}}\bigr)
=
\bigl(L^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}}\setminus0\bigr)
/\mathbb R_{>0}
\]
the corresponding $\mathbb Z_2$-torsor.

Then there is a canonical isomorphism
\[
O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}}
\cong
O\bigl(L^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}}\bigr).
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
\textbf{Step 1.} It is enough to prove this in the case of a trivial family
$\pi$.

Then one has the following commutative diagram:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}\label{ConFl}
	{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\mathbb R,\rm cs}} &&
	{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}} \\
	\\
	{U\times KO} && {U\times KU}
	\arrow["c", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\pi_!^{KO}}"', from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["{\pi_!^{KU,\mathrm{spin}}}", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{id}_U\times c}"', from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
This is the so-called ``Atiyah--Bott--Shapiro square.'' It commutes because
the restriction of the $\operatorname{Spin}^c$ orientation of $KU$ along
$\operatorname{Spin}\to\operatorname{Spin}^c$ is the complexification of the
spin orientation of $KO$.\footnote{In the rest of the present paper, we use
the word \textit{orientation} in a different sense.} See \cite{CF}, going back
to \cite{ABS}. For a modern treatment, see \cite{HK}. Since the relative
Calabi--Yau structure trivializes the relative canonical bundle,
\eqref{complex-spin-pushforward} identifies the right vertical map with
$\pi_!^{KU,\mathbb C}$.

The statement therefore follows from Steps 2 and 3 below.

\textbf{Step 2.} As we already mentioned, \textit{topological Serre duality} (see
\cite{Miller}, \cite{Dyer}, and, for a categorification,
\cite[Appendix A]{Karpov}) asserts that the following diagram commutes:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}} &
	{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\rm cs}} \\
	{U\times KU} & {U\times KU}
	\arrow["{(-)^\vee}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\pi_!^{KU,\mathbb C}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\pi_!^{KU,\mathbb C}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{(-)^\vee}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where both the upper and lower horizontal arrows are induced by the relative
duality map.

It has a natural real counterpart, which is proved analogously:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\mathbb R,\rm cs}} &
	{\mathcal C_{\mathfrak X/U}^{\mathbb R,\rm cs}} \\
	{U\times KO} & {U\times KO}
	\arrow["{(-)^\vee}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\pi_!^{KO}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\pi_!^{KO}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{(-)^\vee}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\]

The Atiyah--Bott--Shapiro square above and
\eqref{complex-spin-pushforward} prove that the complex and real duality
diagrams are compatible. The lemma therefore follows from the following
elementary linear-algebraic statement.

\textbf{Step 3.} Let $V$ be a real one-dimensional vector space, and let
$V_{\mathbb C}$ be its complexification. Suppose that $V$ is equipped with a
non-degenerate pairing $\iota:V\otimes V\to\mathbb R$.

Denote by $\omega(\iota)$ the set of isomorphisms
$\kappa:V_{\mathbb C}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb C$ for which the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
	{V_{\mathbb C}\otimes V_{\mathbb C}} & {\mathbb C} \\
	{\mathbb C\otimes\mathbb C} & {\mathbb C}
	\arrow["{\iota_{\mathbb C}}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\kappa\otimes\kappa}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\operatorname{Id}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["m"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commutes.

Then there is a natural equivalence of $\mathbb Z_2$-torsors
\[
V/\mathbb R_{>0}\cong\omega(\iota).
\]
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{closedcobordism}
Consider two closed smooth spin $8$-folds $X_1$ and $X_2$.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(a)] Let $\phi_i\in\mathcal C_{X_i}$ for $i=1,2$. Suppose that there
exists a spin bordism $W$ from $X_1$ to $X_2$, together with an element
$\phi\in\mathcal C_W$, which restricts to $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ on the
components of
\[
\partial W=-X_1\sqcup X_2,
\]
respectively. Then these data give rise to a canonical identification of
$\mathbb Z_2$-torsors
\[
\iota_{[W,\phi]}:
O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{X_1}}|_{\phi_1}
\xrightarrow{\sim}
O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{X_2}}|_{\phi_2}.
\]

\item[\rm(b)] Let
$\psi_i\in\mathcal C_{X_i}^{\mathbb R}$ for $i=1,2$. Suppose that there exists
a spin bordism $W$ from $X_1$ to $X_2$, together with an element
$\psi\in\mathcal C_W^{\mathbb R}$, which restricts to $\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$
on the components of $\partial W=-X_1\sqcup X_2$, respectively. Then these
data give rise to a canonical identification of $\mathbb Z_2$-torsors
\[
\iota^{KO}_{[W,\psi]}:
O^{KO}_{\mathcal C_{X_1}^{\mathbb R}}|_{\psi_1}
\xrightarrow{\sim}
O^{KO}_{\mathcal C_{X_2}^{\mathbb R}}|_{\psi_2}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
It is enough to prove part~\textup{(b)}. Indeed, part~\textup{(a)} then follows
by pulling back along the map $\operatorname{Ad}$. We use the ideas of
Carvalho's argument; see \cite{Carvalho}.

\textbf{Step 1.} First, choose small collars $C_1$ and $C_2$ of the boundary
components in $W$. For $N$ sufficiently large, there
exists a neat embedding
\[
e:W\longrightarrow [0,1]\times\mathbb R^N
\]
which is also of product form on the collars. This follows from the relative
Whitney embedding theorem.

\textbf{Step 2.} As in the construction of
Subsection~\ref{sec:push}, one obtains a natural Pontryagin--Thom collapse map
\[
c:[0,1]_+\wedge S^N\longrightarrow\operatorname{Th}(\nu_e),
\]
whose restrictions to the boundary are the Pontryagin--Thom collapse maps
\[
c_0:\{0\}_+\wedge S^N\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Th}(\nu_e|_{X_1}),
\qquad
c_1:\{1\}_+\wedge S^N\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Th}(\nu_e|_{X_2}).
\]

Combining $c$ with the $KO$-theory Thom class and the class $\psi$, one may
interpret it as a path in $KO$ between
$\pi_{X_1!}^{KO}(\psi_1)$ and $\pi_{X_2!}^{KO}(\psi_2)$. Applying the real
determinant therefore gives the desired isomorphism.

\textbf{Step 3.} It remains to show that the isomorphism constructed in
Step~2 is canonical. For this, it is enough to show that the data used in
Step~1 (the collars, the tubular neighbourhood, and the neat embedding with
product structure on the collars) are unique up to homotopy after
stabilization. This is standard; see, for example, \cite[p.~22]{GMTW}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $(Y,A)$ be a topological pair. A \textit{relative $n$-bordism over
$(Y,A)$} consists of the following data:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Two smooth $n$-manifolds, possibly with boundary, say
$(M_0,\partial M_0)$ and $(M_1,\partial M_1)$, equipped with maps
$f_i:M_i\to Y$ satisfying $f_i(\partial M_i)\subseteq A$ for $i=0,1$.
\item A smooth $(n+1)$-manifold $W$ with corners, together with a decomposition
of its codimension-one boundary faces
\[
\partial W\cong -M_0\cup M_1\cup Q,
\]
where $Q$ is the relative boundary face which intersects with each of $M_i$ by its boundary, and a map $f_W:W\to Y$ such that
$f_W|_{M_i}=f_i$ for $i=0,1$ and $f_W(Q)\subseteq A$.
\end{enumerate}
This definition generalizes in the evident way to relative spin bordisms and
other tangential structures.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
For a compact manifold $X$, possibly with non-empty boundary, write
\[
\mathcal C_X^{\rm cs}
=\operatorname{Map}_*(X/\partial X,BU\times\mathbb Z),
\qquad
\mathcal C_X^{\mathbb R,\rm cs}
=\operatorname{Map}_*(X/\partial X,BO\times\mathbb Z).
\]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{relative-cobordism-invariance}
Consider two compact smooth spin $8$-manifolds $X_1$ and $X_2$, possibly
with boundary, and classes $\phi_i\in\mathcal C_{X_i}^{\rm cs}$.

Suppose that there is a relative spin bordism $(W,\phi)$ from
$(X_1,\phi_1)$ to $(X_2,\phi_2)$ over
$(BU\times\mathbb Z,0)$. Then these data give rise to a canonical
identification of $\mathbb Z_2$-torsors
\[
\iota_{[W,\phi]}:
O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{X_1}^{\rm cs}}|_{\phi_1}
\xrightarrow{\sim}
O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{X_2}^{\rm cs}}|_{\phi_2}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
A \emph{Picard groupoid} is a symmetric monoidal category
\[
(\mathcal G,\otimes,1,\alpha,\sigma)
\]
in which all morphisms are invertible and every object is invertible up to
isomorphism.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{relative-bordism-category}
The \emph{relative spin bordism category over $(\mathbb K,0)$}, denoted by
$
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(\mathbb K,0),
$
is the Picard groupoid defined as follows. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item Its objects are pairs $[X,f]$, where $X$ is a compact collared smooth spin
$8$-manifold with boundary (possibly empty), and $f$ is a continuous map of
pairs
\[
f:(X,\partial X)\longrightarrow(\mathbb K,0).
\]

\item The morphism set
\[
\operatorname{Mor}\bigl([X,f],[Y,g]\bigr)
\]
consists of equivalence classes $[W,k]$ of relative spin bordisms from
$[X,f]$ to $[Y,g]$ over $(\mathbb K,0)$, in the sense of
Subsection~\ref{closed-relative-cobordism}, with $W$ compact and with
corners of codimension at most two. The incoming and outgoing faces are
disjoint and meet the relative face in their boundaries. Their
parametrisations, compatible collars, and product spin identifications
are part of the data. Components without incoming or outgoing faces are
allowed.

\item   Let $(W_0,k_0)$ and $(W_1,k_1)$ be two
representatives of relative spin bordisms from $[X,f]$ to $[Y,g]$.  Thus, for
$i=0,1$, the boundary of $W_i$ is decomposed as
\[
\partial W_i\cong -X\cup Y\cup Q_i,
\qquad k_i(Q_i)\subseteq\{0\},
\]
where $Q_i$ is the relative boundary face, and the restrictions of $k_i$ to
$X$ and $Y$ equal $f$ and $g$, respectively.

We declare
\[
(W_0,k_0)\sim(W_1,k_1)
\]
if there exist a compact spin $10$-manifold $T$ with corners of
codimension at most three, a
continuous map $K:T\to\mathbb K$, and a union $Q_T$ of boundary faces of $T$
such that
\[
\partial T\cong
(-W_0)\cup W_1\cup(X\times I)\cup(-Y\times I)\cup Q_T,
\]
where $I=[0,1]$. The $W_i$-faces are disjoint, as are the two side
faces, and $W_i$ meets them in $X\times\{i\}$ and $Y\times\{i\}$.

The remaining intersections are
\[
Q_T\cap W_i=Q_i,
\qquad
Q_T\cap(X\times I)=\partial X\times I,
\qquad
Q_T\cap(Y\times I)=\partial Y\times I.
\]
We require
\[
K(Q_T)\subseteq\{0\},
\qquad
K|_{W_i}=k_i\quad(i=0,1),
\]
and require
\[
K|_{X\times I}=f\circ\operatorname{pr}_X,
\qquad
K|_{Y\times I}=g\circ\operatorname{pr}_Y.
\]

The notation $[W,k]$ means the equivalence class of $(W,k)$ under this
relation.

\item If
\[
[W,k]:[X,f]\longrightarrow[Y,g],
\qquad
[V,l]:[Y,g]\longrightarrow[Z,h],
\]
their composite is represented by
\[
W\cup_{Y\times\{0\}}(Y\times I)
 \cup_{Y\times\{1\}}V,
\]
with map equal to $k$, $g\circ\operatorname{pr}_Y$, and $l$ on the
three pieces, respectively. The identity of $[X,f]$ is
represented by
\[
[X\times I,f\circ\operatorname{pr}_X].
\]


\item The monoidal structure is given by disjoint union.  On objects,
\[
[X,f]\otimes[X',f']=[X\sqcup X',f\sqcup f'].
\]
On morphisms,
\[
[W,k]\otimes[W',k']=[W\sqcup W',k\sqcup k'].
\]
The relative boundary face is $Q_W\sqcup Q_{W'}$, whose image lies in
$\{0\}$.

\item The monoidal identity is
\[
\mathbf 1=[\varnothing, \varnothing].
\]

\item The dual of $[X,f]$ is
\[
[X,f]^*=[-X,f],
\]
where $-X$ denotes $X$ with the opposite spin structure.  The evaluation
morphism
\[
[-X,f]\otimes[X,f]\longrightarrow\mathbf 1
\]
is represented by the cylinder
\[
[X\times I,f\circ\operatorname{pr}_X],
\]
whose relative boundary face $\partial X\times I$ is mapped to $0$.

\item The symmetry isomorphism
\[
\sigma_{[X,f],[Y,g]}:
[X,f]\otimes[Y,g]\longrightarrow[Y,g]\otimes[X,f]
\]
is represented by
\[
\bigl[(X\sqcup Y)\times I,
      (f\sqcup g)\circ\operatorname{pr}_{X\sqcup Y}\bigr],
\]
where the incoming boundary is identified with $X\sqcup Y$ and the outgoing
boundary with $Y\sqcup X$ by transposing the two components.  The relative
boundary face $(\partial X\sqcup\partial Y)\times I$ is mapped to $0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item The same definition gives a Picard groupoid
\(
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(V,A)
\)
for any topological pair $(V,A)$.
\item Although we restrict here to $8$-manifolds, the same constructions are
meaningful for $7$-manifolds, as in the original work of Joyce and Upmeier
\cite{JU}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{global-orientation-functor}
For an object $[X,f]$, define
\[
\mathrm O_8^{\operatorname{Spin},{\rm c}}[X,f]
=
\left(
\operatorname{ind}_X(f)\bmod2,
O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_X^{\rm cs}}|_f
\right),
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{ind}_X(f)
=\pi_{X!}^{KO}\bigl(\operatorname{Ad}_X(f)\bigr)
\in KO^0(\operatorname{pt})\cong\mathbb Z
\]
uses the notation of Subsection~\ref{sec:push}.  For a morphism
$[W,k]:[X,f]\to[Y,g]$, put
\[
\mathrm O_8^{\operatorname{Spin},{\rm c}}[W,k]=\iota_{[W,k]}:
O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_X^{\rm cs}}|_f
\xrightarrow{\sim}
O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_Y^{\rm cs}}|_g.
\]
Proposition~\ref{relative-cobordism-invariance} shows that this is
well-defined and functorial.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{fixed-bordism-category}
Let $X$ be a compact collared spin $8$-manifold with boundary.  Define
\(
\operatorname{Bord}_X(\mathbb K,0)
\)
as follows.

The objects are maps of pairs
\[
f:(X,\partial X)\longrightarrow(\mathbb K,0).
\]
For two objects $f_0,f_1$, a morphism
\[
[H]:f_0\longrightarrow f_1
\]
is an equivalence class of maps
\[
H:X\times I\longrightarrow\mathbb K
\]
satisfying
\[
H|_{X\times\{0\}}=f_0,
\qquad
H|_{X\times\{1\}}=f_1,
\qquad
H(\partial X\times I)=\{0\}.
\]
Two such homotopies $H,H':f_0\to f_1$ are equivalent if there is a map
\[
K:X\times I\times I\longrightarrow\mathbb K
\]
such that
\[
K(x,t,0)=H(x,t),
\qquad
K(x,t,1)=H'(x,t),
\]
\[
K(x,0,s)=f_0(x),
\qquad
K(x,1,s)=f_1(x),
\]
and
\[
K(a,t,s)=0
\quad\text{for all }a\in\partial X, s,t\in I.
\]

Composition is given by concatenation.  The identity of $f$ is represented by
$f\circ\operatorname{pr}_X$, and the inverse of $[H]$ by
$H^{-1}(x,t)=H(x,1-t)$.  Thus $\operatorname{Bord}_X(\mathbb K,0)$ is a
groupoid.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{Picgroup}
The same definition gives categories
$\operatorname{Bord}_X(V,A)$ for a topological pair $(V,A)$.  Choices that
will be important below include $(BU(m),0)$ and $(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{openBordX}
Let $X$ be a smooth, possibly non-compact, spin $8$-manifold.  Define
\(
\operatorname{Bord}_X^{\rm cs}(\mathbb K)
\)
as follows.  Its objects are compactly supported maps $f:X\to\mathbb K$.
For two objects $f_0,f_1$, a morphism $[H]:f_0\to f_1$ is an equivalence
class of compactly supported maps
\[
H:X\times I\longrightarrow\mathbb K
\]
such that $H|_{X\times\{i\}}=f_i$ for $i=0,1$.  Here compact support means
that there is a compact set $K\subset X$ such that
$H|(X\setminus K)\times I=0$.

Two such homotopies $H,H'$ are equivalent if there exists a compactly
supported map
\[
\Lambda:X\times I\times I\longrightarrow\mathbb K
\]
satisfying
\[
\Lambda(x,t,0)=H(x,t),
\qquad
\Lambda(x,t,1)=H'(x,t),
\]
\[
\Lambda(x,0,s)=f_0(x),
\qquad
\Lambda(x,1,s)=f_1(x).
\]
Composition, identities, and inverses are defined as above.  Thus
$\operatorname{Bord}_X^{\rm cs}(\mathbb K)$ is a groupoid.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{open-Pi-functor}
Let $X$ be as in Definition~\ref{openBordX}.  There is a natural functor
\[
\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin},{\rm cs}}:
\operatorname{Bord}_X^{\rm cs}(\mathbb K)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(\mathbb K,0).
\]
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We first define $\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin},{\rm cs}}$ on objects.  Let
$f:X\to\mathbb K$ be
compactly supported.  Choose a compact codimension-zero submanifold
$X'\subset X$ with boundary such that
\[
f|_{X\setminus\operatorname{int}(X')}=0,
\]
and set
\[
\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin},{\rm cs}}(f)=[X',f|_{X'}].
\]
On morphisms, use a compact codimension-zero submanifold containing the
support of the homotopy.  Independence of these choices follows from the
excision trick in Subsection~\ref{bordcatextr}; compatibility with
composition is immediate.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{orientation-fixed-X}
Let $X$ be a spin $8$-manifold, either compact with boundary or open.  Write
$F_X^\dagger$ for the corresponding functor above, and let
\[
\mathbf 1_X:
\operatorname{Bord}_X^\dagger(\mathbb K)
\longrightarrow\mathbb Z_2\text{-tor}
\]
be the constant functor with value the trivial $\mathbb Z_2$-torsor
$\mathbb Z_2$.  An \emph{orientation for $X$} is a natural
isomorphism
\[
\omega_X:F_X^\dagger\Longrightarrow\mathbf 1_X.
\]
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
The natural isomorphism $\omega_X$ should be regarded as a
bordism-coherent trivialization of the topological orientation bundle.  In
particular, evaluating $\omega_X$ on objects gives a trivialization of
$O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_X^{\rm cs}}$.  This is the compactly supported
analogue of the discussion in \cite[Section 4]{JU}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{homgrgr}
The following isomorphisms hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $m\geq5$,
\[
\pi_0\!\left(
  \operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BSU(m),*)
\right)
\cong
\widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BSU(m))
\cong\mathbb Z^3,
\]
and
\[
\pi_1\!\left(
  \operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BSU(m),*)
\right)
\cong
\widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_9(BSU(m))
\cong\mathbb Z_2.
\]

\item
\[
\pi_0\!\left(
  \operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
\right)
\cong\mathbb Z^2,
\qquad
\pi_1\!\left(
  \operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
\right)
\cong\mathbb Z_2.
\]

\item
\[
\pi_0\!\left(
  \operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BE_8,*)
\right)
\cong\mathbb Z^2,
\qquad
\pi_1\!\left(
  \operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BE_8,*)
\right)
\cong\mathbb Z_2.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Joyce and Upmeier prove that
\[
\pi_i\!\left(\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(T)\right)
\cong
\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_{8+i}(T),
\qquad i=0,1;
\]
see \cite[Proposition~7.2, equations~(7.2)--(7.3)]{JU}.  The same argument for
the relative category of Definition~\ref{relative-bordism-category} gives
\[
\pi_i\!\left(
  \operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(T,*)
\right)
\cong
\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_{8+i}(T,*)
\cong
\widetilde\Omega^{\operatorname{Spin}}_{8+i}(T),
\qquad i=0,1,
\]
for any pointed space $(T,*)$.

The stated values for $BSU(m)$ and $BE_8$ are given in
\cite[Corollary~3.4(a), Table~3.4]{JU}; the restriction $m\geq5$ ensures that
the stable calculation applies in both degrees $8$ and $9$.  The values for
$K(\mathbb Z,4)$ are given in \cite[Theorem~3.1(a), Table~3.1]{JU}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{generators}
The argument of Joyce and Upmeier not only calculates the relevant bordism
groups, but also gives distinguished generators.  To distinguish the three
cases, we add superscripts, which are suppressed in \cite{JU} when the
ambient space is clear:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\frac{\zeta_1^{SU}}2,\zeta_2^{SU},\zeta_3^{SU}$ generate $\pi_0$ in
the $SU(m)$ case, and $\alpha_1\zeta_2^{SU}$ generates $\pi_1$;
\item $\zeta_2^{E_8},\zeta_3^{E_8}$ generate $\pi_0$ in the $E_8$ case, and
$\alpha_1\zeta_2^{E_8}$ generates $\pi_1$;
\item $\zeta_2^K,\zeta_3^K$ generate $\pi_0$ in the $K(\mathbb Z,4)$ case,
and $\alpha_1\zeta_2^K$ generates $\pi_1$.
\end{enumerate}
Their geometric definitions are too intricate to reproduce here; see
\cite[Theorem~3.1, Corollary~3.4 and Tables~3.1, 3.4]{JU}.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{E8-explicit-orientation-functor}
There is a monoidal natural isomorphism
\[
\widetilde{\mathrm N}_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},E_8,{\rm c}}
\cong
\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},E_8,{\rm c}}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The proof is the compactly supported version of the calculation in
\cite[Theorem~11.1, Tables~11.1--11.2]{JU}.  That calculation is topological
and uses the Atiyah--Singer Index Theorem. It applies
\textit{mutatis mutandis} to our relative bordism categories and gives the maps on $\pi_0$
and $\pi_1$ displayed above.  The classification theorem of
Subsection~\ref{picardgen} then gives the required monoidal natural
isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{orientation-conventions}
The monoidal natural isomorphism \(\lambda_8^{\rm c}\) in \eqref{E8Z4}
is not canonical.  In the compact theory, Joyce and Upmeier show that the
choices compatible with the functors to and from
\(\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(*)\) form a torsor for
\(\mathbb Z_2^2\); a choice is what they call an orientation convention
\cite[Theorem~11.10(a) and Remark~12.16(c)]{JU}.  We impose the same
compatibility on \(\lambda_8^{\rm c}\) and fix one such isomorphism.  The
functor \(\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},E_8,{\rm c}}\) is
identified with \(\widetilde{\mathrm N}_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{
\operatorname{Spin},E_8,{\rm c}}\) using
Proposition~\ref{E8-explicit-orientation-functor}; changing this
identification is included in the choice of \(\lambda_8^{\rm c}\).  The
isomorphisms \(\lambda_{8,m}^{\operatorname{SU},{\rm c}}\) and
\(\lambda_{8,m}^{\operatorname{U},{\rm c}}\) below always mean those obtained
from this choice in Lemma~\ref{rescompc} and
Proposition~\ref{BU-BSU-transition}.

We also use this opportunity to fix some complex structures used in Lemma~\ref{comptype}.  Let
\(\pi_v:\operatorname{Spin}(16)\to\operatorname{SO}(16)\) and
\(\pi_s:\operatorname{Spin}(16)\to
\operatorname{HSpin}(16)\) be the quotient maps, and put
\(\widetilde{\operatorname{U}}(8)=
\pi_v^{-1}(\operatorname{U}(8))\) and
\(U=\pi_s(\widetilde{\operatorname{U}}(8))\).  The homomorphism
\((A,\zeta)\mapsto\zeta A\) from
\(\operatorname{SU}(8)\times\operatorname{U}(1)\) to
\(\operatorname{U}(8)\) lifts to \(\widetilde{\operatorname{U}}(8)\).
Indeed, under the determinant isomorphism
\(\pi_1(\operatorname{U}(8))\cong\mathbb Z\), its image is
\(8\mathbb Z\), which maps to zero in
\(\pi_1(\operatorname{SO}(16))\cong\mathbb Z_2\).
Its composite with \(\pi_s\) is a finite covering onto \(U\).  We take
\(\iota_8:\operatorname{SU}(8)\times\operatorname{U}(1)\to E_8\) to be
this covering followed by the inclusions
\(U\subset\operatorname{HSpin}(16)\subset E_8\); compare
\cite[Chapters~6--7]{AdamsExceptional}. This is a representative
of the morphism of complex type of \cite[Theorem~11.8]{JU} used in
Lemma~\ref{rescompc} to construct
\(\lambda_{8,8}^{\operatorname{SU},{\rm c}}\) from \(\lambda_8^{\rm c}\).

We choose the complex structure on \(\mathfrak e_8/\mathfrak u(8)\) whose
restriction to \(\operatorname{SU}(8)\) is
\(W\oplus\Lambda^3W\oplus(\Lambda^2W)^\vee\), where \(W\) is the standard
representation.  For
\(\jmath_m(A)=\operatorname{diag}(A,\det(A)^{-1})\), we regard the quotient
representation as the underlying real representation of
\(W_m\otimes\det(W_m)\), where \(W_m\) is the standard representation of
\(\operatorname{U}(m)\).  These complex structures are used throughout. 

It is easy to see that the  choice of \(\lambda_8^{\rm c}\) does not affect the 
calculations in the present paper.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{complex-type-morphism}
Let $G_1,G_2$ be compact Lie groups, and let
\(
\iota:G_1\longrightarrow G_2
\)
be a morphism of Lie groups. Write $\mathfrak g_1,\mathfrak g_2$ for their
Lie algebras and
\(
d\iota:\mathfrak g_1\longrightarrow\mathfrak g_2
\)
for the induced Lie algebra morphism. We say that $\iota$ is a
\emph{morphism of complex type} if $d\iota$ is injective and the quotient
\(
\mathfrak m_\iota:=\mathfrak g_2/d\iota(\mathfrak g_1)
\)
is of complex type as a real $G_1$-representation. Equivalently, there is an
endomorphism
\(
J:\mathfrak m_\iota\longrightarrow\mathfrak m_\iota,
\ J^2=-1,
\)
which commutes with the $G_1$-action induced by the adjoint action of $G_2$
through $\iota$. Thus $\mathfrak m_\iota$ is the underlying real
representation of a complex $G_1$-representation. This is the terminology of
\cite[Definition~11.5]{JU}.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{comptype}
Let $\iota:G_1\to G_2$ be a morphism of complex type, and let
\[
F_\iota^{\rm c}:
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BG_1,*)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BG_2,*)
\]
be the transfer functor induced by $B\iota$. There is a canonical monoidal
natural isomorphism
\[
\epsilon_\iota^{\rm c}:
\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},G_1,{\rm c}}
\Longrightarrow
\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},G_2,{\rm c}}
\circ F_\iota^{\rm c}.
\]
Equivalently, the following diagram is $2$-commutative:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=6.7em,row sep=3em]
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BG_1,*)
  \arrow[r,"{F_\iota^{\rm c}}"]
  \arrow[d,"{\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},G_1,{\rm c}}}"']
  \arrow[dr,phantom,"\Downarrow\,\epsilon_\iota^{\rm c}" description]
&
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BG_2,*)
  \arrow[d,"{\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},G_2,{\rm c}}}"]
\\
\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2
  \arrow[r,"\operatorname{id}"']
&
\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Over $BG_1$ there is a natural decomposition
\[
(B\iota)^*\bigl(
 \operatorname{Ad}(\mathfrak g_2)-\underline{\mathfrak g_2}
\bigr)
\cong
\operatorname{Ad}(\mathfrak g_1)-\underline{\mathfrak g_1}
\oplus
\bigl(
 \mathfrak m_\iota-\underline{\mathfrak m_\iota}
\bigr).
\]
The second summand is the underlying real bundle of a virtual complex bundle.
The rest follows as in \cite[Proposition~11.6(a),(c)]{JU} using the Atiyah--Bott--Shapiro square of Section \ref{KO-theoretic-interpretation}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{product-and-abelian}
The normalized orientation functors have the following properties.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $G_1,G_2$ be compact Lie groups, let
$\pi_i:G_1\times G_2\to G_i$ be the projections, and let
$F_{\pi_i}^{\rm c}$ be the induced transfer functors. There is a canonical
monoidal natural isomorphism $\zeta_{G_1,G_2}^{\rm c}$ making the following
diagram $2$-commutative:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=8em,row sep=3em]
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(B(G_1\times G_2),*)
  \arrow[r,"{\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},G_1\times G_2,{\rm c}}}"]
  \arrow[d,"{(F_{\pi_1}^{\rm c},F_{\pi_2}^{\rm c})}"']
  \arrow[dr,phantom,"\Downarrow\,\zeta_{G_1,G_2}^{\rm c}" description]
&
\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2
\\
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BG_1,*)\times\\
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BG_2,*)
\end{gathered}
  \arrow[r,"{\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},G_1,{\rm c}}
  \times
  \mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},G_2,{\rm c}}}"']
&
(\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2)\times(\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2)
  \arrow[u,"\otimes"'].
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\item If $G$ is abelian, there is a canonical monoidal natural isomorphism
\[
\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},G,{\rm c}}
\cong\mathbf 1,
\]
where $\mathbf 1$ is the constant functor with value the monoidal identity of
$\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The first statement follows from the canonical direct sum decomposition of
the reduced adjoint virtual bundle and the compatibility of determinant
torsors with direct sums. If $G$ is abelian, its adjoint action on
$\mathfrak g$ is trivial, so the reduced adjoint virtual bundle is canonically
zero. These identifications are compatible with relative bordisms, compare
\cite[Proposition~11.6(b)--(d)]{JU}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{rescompc}
For every $m\geq2$, there is a monoidal natural isomorphism
\[
\lambda_{8,m}^{\operatorname{SU},{\rm c}}:
\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},\operatorname{SU}(m),{\rm c}}
\Longrightarrow
\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}
\circ F_{B\operatorname{SU}(m)}^{K(\mathbb Z,4),{\rm c}},
\]
where
\[
F_{B\operatorname{SU}(m)}^{K(\mathbb Z,4),{\rm c}}:
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(B\operatorname{SU}(m),*)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
\]
is induced by $c_2:B\operatorname{SU}(m)\to K(\mathbb Z,4)$. Equivalently,
the following diagram is $2$-commutative:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7.8em,row sep=3em]
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(B\operatorname{SU}(m),*)
  \arrow[r,"{F_{B\operatorname{SU}(m)}^{K(\mathbb Z,4),{\rm c}}}"]
  \arrow[d,"{\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},\operatorname{SU}(m),{\rm c}}}"']
  \arrow[dr,phantom,"\Downarrow\,\lambda_{8,m}^{\operatorname{SU},{\rm c}}" description]
&
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
  \arrow[d,"{\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}}"]
\\
\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2
  \arrow[r,"\operatorname{id}"']
&
\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We follow the proof of \cite[Theorem~11.11(a)(i),(b)(i)]{JU}.

\textit{Step 1.}
Consider the $2$-commutative diagram~\eqref{E8Z4}. Joyce and Upmeier construct
a morphism of complex type
\[
\iota_8:\operatorname{SU}(8)\times\operatorname{U}(1)
\longrightarrow E_8;
\]
see \cite[Theorem~11.8]{JU}. Lemmas~\ref{comptype} and
\ref{product-and-abelian}, together with diagram~\eqref{E8Z4}, therefore give
the required factorization for $\operatorname{SU}(8)$. With the normalizations
of Joyce and Upmeier, the composite
\[
B\operatorname{SU}(8)
\longrightarrow BE_8
\xrightarrow{a_1}K(\mathbb Z,4)
\]
represents $c_2$; compare \cite[Remark~8.2(a), Theorem~11.11(b)(i), and its
proof]{JU}.

\textit{Step 2.}
For $2\leq m<8$, use the complex-type morphisms
\[
\operatorname{SU}(m)\times\operatorname{U}(1)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{SU}(m+1)
\]
of \cite[Theorem~11.8]{JU}, together with
Lemmas~\ref{comptype} and~\ref{product-and-abelian}. The pullback of $c_2$
under the standard inclusion
$B\operatorname{SU}(m)\to B\operatorname{SU}(m+1)$ is again $c_2$, so the
factorization descends from $m+1$ to $m$.

For $m>8$, the stabilization maps
$B\operatorname{SU}(m)\to B\operatorname{SU}(m+1)$ induce equivalences on the
spin bordism categories in dimensions $8$ and $9$. Since $c_2$ is stable, the
factorization for $m=8$ therefore extends to every $m>8$. See
\cite[Theorem~3.3(b), Theorem~8.3(b), and the proof of
Theorem~11.11(b)(i)]{JU}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{BU-BSU-transition}
For $m\geq1$, define
\[
\jmath_m:\operatorname{U}(m)\longrightarrow\operatorname{SU}(m+1),
\qquad
A\longmapsto
\begin{pmatrix}
A&0\\
0&\det(A)^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This is a morphism of complex type. On classifying spaces, $B\jmath_m$ sends a
rank-$m$ complex vector bundle $E$ to
\(
E\oplus\det(E)^\vee.
\)
Moreover, the diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=6em,row sep=3em]
B\operatorname{U}(m)
  \arrow[r,"{B\jmath_m}"]
  \arrow[dr,"{\kappa_m=c_2-c_1^2}"']
&
B\operatorname{SU}(m+1)
  \arrow[d,"c_2"]
\\
&K(\mathbb Z,4)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commutes up to homotopy. Consequently, there is a monoidal natural
isomorphism
\[
\lambda_{8,m}^{\operatorname{U},{\rm c}}:
\mathrm N_{8,\mathbb Z_2}^{\operatorname{Spin},\operatorname{U}(m),{\rm c}}
\Longrightarrow
\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}
\circ F_{B\operatorname{U}(m)}^{K(\mathbb Z,4),{\rm c}},
\]
where the transfer functor on the right is induced by
$\kappa_m=c_2-c_1^2$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The fact that $\jmath_m$ is of complex type follows from
\cite[Theorem~11.8]{JU}. Hence Lemma~\ref{comptype} compares the normalized
$\operatorname{U}(m)$-orientation functor with the pullback of the normalized
$\operatorname{SU}(m+1)$-orientation functor. For a rank $m$ bundle $E$, the
Whitney formula gives
\[
c_1\bigl(E\oplus\det(E)^\vee\bigr)=0,
\qquad
c_2\bigl(E\oplus\det(E)^\vee\bigr)
=c_2(E)-c_1(E)^2.
\]
The result now follows by composing the natural isomorphism of
Lemma~\ref{comptype} with $\lambda_{8,m+1}^{\operatorname{SU},{\rm c}}$ from
Lemma~\ref{rescompc}. This is the $\operatorname{U}(m)$ step in the proof of
\cite[Theorem~11.11(b)(i)]{JU}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cantriv}
Let $X$ be a complex $4$-fold equipped with a spin structure, which is either
compact, possibly with boundary, or open. Put
\[
X^\dagger=
\begin{cases}
X/\partial X,&X\text{ compact},\\
X^+,&X\text{ open},
\end{cases}
\qquad
\mathcal C_{X,0}^\dagger=
\operatorname{Map}_*(X^\dagger,BU),
\]
where, if $\partial X=\varnothing$, a disjoint basepoint is understood, and
$BU$ is the virtual-rank-zero component of $BU\times\mathbb Z$.

Assume that the ungraded cohomology orientation functor
\[
\Pi_{\mathbb Z_2\text{-tor}}
\circ\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}
\circ\Pi_X^\dagger:
\operatorname{Bord}_X^\dagger(K(\mathbb Z,4))
\longrightarrow\mathbb Z_2\text{-tor}
\]
admits a trivialization. Here $\operatorname{Bord}_X^\dagger$ and
$\Pi_X^\dagger$ use the compact/open convention of
Subsection~\ref{orfun}. Then the restriction of $F_X^\dagger$ to the
virtual-rank-zero mapping space $\mathcal C_{X,0}^\dagger$ is orientable.
Equivalently, the normalized determinant $\mathbb Z_2$-bundle over
$\operatorname{Map}_*(X^\dagger,BU)$ is trivial.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let
\[
j_m:
\operatorname{Map}_*(X^\dagger,B\operatorname{U}(m))
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Map}_*(X^\dagger,BU)
\]
be induced by stabilization. Proposition~\ref{BU-BSU-transition} identifies
the restriction of the normalized orientation functor along $j_m$ with the
pullback of the cohomology orientation functor along
\[
\kappa_m=c_2-c_1^2:
B\operatorname{U}(m)\longrightarrow K(\mathbb Z,4).
\]
The assumed trivialization therefore shows that the normalized determinant
$\mathbb Z_2$-bundle is trivial after pullback along every $j_m$.

It remains only to pass to the stable mapping space. The space $X^\dagger$ is
compact, and $BU=\operatorname*{colim}_mB\operatorname{U}(m)$ has its usual
CW topology. Hence every singular $1$-simplex in
$\operatorname{Map}_*(X^\dagger,BU)$, equivalently every map
\[
X^\dagger\times\Delta^1\longrightarrow BU,
\]
has image in $B\operatorname{U}(m)$ for some $m$. It follows that
\[
H_1\bigl(\operatorname{Map}_*(X^\dagger,BU);\mathbb Z_2\bigr)
=
\operatorname*{colim}_m
H_1\bigl(
 \operatorname{Map}_*(X^\dagger,B\operatorname{U}(m));\mathbb Z_2
\bigr).
\]
The first Stiefel--Whitney class of the normalized determinant bundle vanishes
on every term on the right, and therefore vanishes on the stable mapping
space. This is precisely orientability in the sense of
Definition~\ref{orientation-fixed-X}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{Steenrodprop}
Let $X$ be a compact spin $8$-manifold with boundary. Suppose that there is no
class $\alpha\in H^3(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z)$ such that
\[
\left\langle
 \bar\alpha\smile\operatorname{Sq}_\partial^2(\bar\alpha),
 [X,\partial X]
\right\rangle
=1
\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z_2,
\]
where $\bar\alpha$ is the mod-$2$ reduction of $\alpha$. Then one may choose a
natural isomorphism $\eta_X^\partial$ making the following diagram
$2$-commutative:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em,row sep=3em]
\operatorname{Bord}_X(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
  \arrow[r,"{\mathbf 1_X}"]
  \arrow[d,"{\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin}}}"']
  \arrow[dr,phantom,"\Downarrow\,\eta_X^\partial" description]
&
0//\mathbb Z_2
\\
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
  \arrow[r,"{\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}}"']
&
\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2
  \arrow[u,"{\Pi_{\mathbb Z_2\text{-tor}}}"'].
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The fundamental groupoid of
$\operatorname{Map}_*(X/\partial X,K(\mathbb Z,4))$ has homotopy groups
\[
\pi_i\operatorname{Map}_*(X/\partial X,K(\mathbb Z,4))
\cong H^{4-i}(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z),
\qquad i=0,1.
\]
With this replacement of absolute by relative cohomology, the proof of
\cite[Theorem~10.7(a) and Subsection~19.2]{JU} applies unchanged. Its
obstruction is exactly
$\langle\bar\alpha\smile\operatorname{Sq}_\partial^2(\bar\alpha),
[X,\partial X]\rangle$. The relative bordism identifications needed in that
proof are supplied by Definition~\ref{fixed-bordism-category} and
Proposition~\ref{relative-cobordism-invariance}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{compactly-supported-Steenrod-trivialization}
Let $X$ be a smooth open spin $8$-manifold. Suppose that there is no class
$\alpha\in H_c^3(X;\mathbb Z)$ such that
\[
\int_X
\bar\alpha\smile\operatorname{Sq}_c^2(\bar\alpha)
=1
\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z_2.
\]
Then one may choose a natural isomorphism $\eta_X^{\rm cs}$ making the
following diagram $2$-commutative:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em,row sep=3em]
\operatorname{Bord}_X^{\rm cs}(K(\mathbb Z,4))
  \arrow[r,"{\mathbf 1_X}"]
  \arrow[d,"{\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin},{\rm cs}}}"']
  \arrow[dr,phantom,"\Downarrow\,\eta_X^{\rm cs}" description]
&
0//\mathbb Z_2
\\
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
  \arrow[r,"{\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}}"']
&
\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2
  \arrow[u,"{\Pi_{\mathbb Z_2\text{-tor}}}"'].
\end{tikzcd}
\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{open-Pi-functor}, the compactly supported mapping
groupoid maps naturally to the relative bordism category. Moreover,
\[
\pi_i\operatorname{Map}_*(X^+,K(\mathbb Z,4))
\cong H_c^{4-i}(X;\mathbb Z),
\qquad i=0,1.
\]
The proof of Proposition~\ref{Steenrodprop} therefore applies verbatim, with
$\operatorname{Sq}_\partial^2$ replaced by $\operatorname{Sq}_c^2$ and the
relative fundamental class replaced by compactly supported integration.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{relative-flag-structure}
Let $X$ be a compact spin $8$-manifold with boundary. A \emph{relative flag
structure} on $(X,\partial X)$ is a natural isomorphism $F$ in the following
$2$-commutative diagram:
\begin{equation}\label{relative-flag-structure-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em,row sep=3em]
\operatorname{Bord}_X(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
  \arrow[r,"{\mathbf 1_X}"]
  \arrow[d,"{\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin}}}"']
  \arrow[dr,phantom,"\Downarrow\,F" description]
&
0//\mathbb Z_2
\\
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
  \arrow[r,"{\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}}"']
&
\mathbb Z_2//\mathbb Z_2
  \arrow[u,"{\Pi_{\mathbb Z_2\text{-tor}}}"'].
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
F:\mathbf 1_X
\Longrightarrow
\Pi_{\mathbb Z_2\text{-tor}}
\circ\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}
\circ\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin}}.
\]

For an open spin $8$-manifold $X$, a \emph{compactly supported flag structure}
is defined by the identical diagram with
$\operatorname{Bord}_X(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)$ and
$\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin}}$ replaced by
$\operatorname{Bord}_X^{\rm cs}(K(\mathbb Z,4))$ and
$\Pi_X^{\operatorname{Spin},{\rm cs}}$, respectively. These are the relative
and compactly supported analogues of \cite[Definition~10.6]{JU}.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{relative-flag-existence-and-classification}
Let $X$ be a compact spin $8$-manifold with boundary.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(a)] The manifold $X$ admits a relative flag structure if and only if
there is no class $\alpha\in H^3(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{relative-flag-obstruction}
\left\langle
 \bar\alpha\smile\operatorname{Sq}_\partial^2(\bar\alpha),
 [X,\partial X]
\right\rangle
=1
\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z_2,
\end{equation}
where $\bar\alpha$ is the mod-$2$ reduction of $\alpha$. If this condition
holds, relative flag structures form a torsor for
\[
\operatorname{Map}
\bigl(H^4(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z_2\bigr),
\]
and relative flag structures natural at zero form a torsor for
\[
\operatorname{Map}
\bigl(H^4(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z)\setminus\{0\},\mathbb Z_2\bigr).
\]

\item[\rm(b)] Relative flag structures factoring via $\mathbb Z_2$ exist if
and only if there is no class $a\in H^3(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z_2)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{relative-flag-obstruction-mod2}
\left\langle
 a\smile\operatorname{Sq}_\partial^2(a),
 [X,\partial X]
\right\rangle
=1.
\end{equation}
Put
\[
I_X^\partial=
\operatorname{Im}\bigl(
 H^4(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z)
 \longrightarrow H^4(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z_2)
\bigr).
\]
If condition~\eqref{relative-flag-obstruction-mod2} holds, relative flag
structures factoring via $\mathbb Z_2$ form a torsor for
$\operatorname{Map}(I_X^\partial,\mathbb Z_2)$, and those which are also
natural at zero form a torsor for
\[
\operatorname{Map}(I_X^\partial\setminus\{0\},\mathbb Z_2).
\]
\end{enumerate}

Here $\operatorname{Map}$ denotes the set of all functions, not only group
homomorphisms. For an open spin $8$-manifold, the identical statements hold
after replacing $H^*(X,\partial X;-)$ by $H_c^*(X;-)$,
$\operatorname{Sq}_\partial^2$ by $\operatorname{Sq}_c^2$, and evaluation on
$[X,\partial X]$ by compactly supported integration. In part~\textup{(b)}, one
then uses
\[
I_X^{\rm c}=
\operatorname{Im}\bigl(
 H_c^4(X;\mathbb Z)
 \longrightarrow H_c^4(X;\mathbb Z_2)
\bigr).
\]
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The existence statements are Proposition~\ref{Steenrodprop} and
Corollary~\ref{compactly-supported-Steenrod-trivialization}. Once one flag
structure is fixed, every other one (with a prescribed value at $0$) differs from it by an automorphism of the
constant functor, hence by an arbitrary function
\[
\pi_0\operatorname{Bord}_X(K(\mathbb Z,4),0)
\longrightarrow\mathbb Z_2.
\]
The first paragraph of this subsection identifies this set of components
with $H^4(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z)$, or with $H_c^4(X;\mathbb Z)$ in the open
case. Naturality at zero fixes the value on the zero component. If the flag
structure factors via $\mathbb Z_2$, only the image of reduction modulo $2$
occurs, giving $I_X^\partial$ or $I_X^{\rm c}$. This is precisely the relative
or compactly supported form of
\cite[Remark~10.5(c)--(d), Definition~10.6, and Theorem~10.7]{JU}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{canonical-orientation-at-zero-class}
Assume that $X$ admits a relative or compactly supported flag structure $F$.
Pulling $F$ back along the sequence
\begin{equation}\label{relative-flag-BU-factorization}
\operatorname{Bord}_X^\dagger(B\operatorname{U}(m))
\xrightarrow{\ B\jmath_m\ }
\operatorname{Bord}_X^\dagger(B\operatorname{SU}(m+1))
\xrightarrow{\ c_2\ }
\operatorname{Bord}_X^\dagger(K(\mathbb Z,4))
\end{equation}
gives an orientation of the restriction of $F_X^\dagger$ to the component of
$E$, or equivalently a cobordism-coherent trivialization of the normalized
determinant $\mathbb Z_2$-torsor on that component. The cohomology class on
which this orientation depends is precisely $\kappa(E)$.

If $F'$ and $F''$ are two such flag structures natural at zero and their ratio
is the function
\[
\epsilon=F''/F':
H^4(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z)\setminus\{0\}
\longrightarrow\mathbb Z_2,
\]
or the analogous function on $H_c^4(X;\mathbb Z)\setminus\{0\}$ in the open
case, then the two induced orientations at $E$ differ by
\begin{equation}\label{relative-flag-orientation-ratio}
(-1)^{\epsilon(\kappa(E))},
\end{equation}
where $\epsilon(0)=0$ by convention, since both structures are natural at
zero. Hence, if
\begin{equation}\label{relative-canonical-integral-condition}
\kappa(E)=c_2(E)-c_1(E)^2=0
\end{equation}
in $H^4(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z)$, or in $H_c^4(X;\mathbb Z)$ in the open case,
the orientation of the component of $E$ is canonical: it is independent of
the choice of a flag structure natural at zero.

If, in addition, condition~\eqref{relative-flag-obstruction-mod2}, or its
compactly supported analogue, holds and we restrict to flag structures
factoring via $\mathbb Z_2$, then it is enough to assume
\begin{equation}\label{relative-canonical-mod2-condition}
\kappa(E)=c_2(E)-c_1(E)^2=0
\end{equation}
in $H^4(X,\partial X;\mathbb Z_2)$, or in $H_c^4(X;\mathbb Z_2)$ in the open
case.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{BU-BSU-transition}, the sequence
\eqref{relative-flag-BU-factorization} sends $E$ to the class
$\kappa(E)=c_2(E)-c_1(E)^2$ and identifies the normalized
$\operatorname{U}(m)$-orientation functor with the pullback of
$\mathrm H_8^{\mathbb Z,{\rm c}}$. Evaluating $F$ at $\kappa(E)$ therefore
gives the asserted orientation.

If $F''/F'=\epsilon$, evaluating the two flag structures at $\kappa(E)$ gives
the sign in \eqref{relative-flag-orientation-ratio}. When $\kappa(E)=0$,
naturality at zero forces the two values to agree. If the structures factor
via $\mathbb Z_2$, the same argument depends only on the mod-$2$ reduction of
$\kappa(E)$. This is the relative or compactly supported version of
\cite[Proposition~12.10(b) and its proof]{JU}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{canonical-Shi-orientation}
Let $Y$ be a smooth complex algebraic $3$-fold, and put
\[
X=\operatorname{Tot}_Y(K_Y),
\qquad
p:X\longrightarrow Y.
\]
Then the determinant line $K_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}$ has a canonical
trivialization compatible with the Serre-duality quadratic form
$Q_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}$. In particular, the orientation bundle
$O^\omega_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}$ has a canonical section.

There is a topological analogue. Put
\[
\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}
=\operatorname{Map}_*(X^+,BU),
\]
as in Corollary~\ref{cantriv}. Then the topological determinant line
$K_{\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}}$ has a canonical trivialization compatible
with $Q_{\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}}$. Thus the topological orientation bundle
$O^{\not D}_{\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}}$ also has a canonical section.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal E$ be the universal perfect complex on
$\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}\times X$, put
$\bar p=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}\times p$, and set
\[
\mathcal G=\mathbf R\bar p_*\mathcal E,
\qquad
\mathcal V=
\mathbf R\pi_{\mathcal M*}
\mathbf R\mathcal Hom(\mathcal G,\mathcal G).
\]
The $p_*\mathcal O_X$-module structure on $\mathcal G$, together with the
tautological section of $p^*K_Y$, gives a canonical triangle
\[
\bar p^*(\mathcal G\otimes K_Y^\vee)
\longrightarrow
\bar p^*\mathcal G
\longrightarrow
\mathcal E
\longrightarrow
\bar p^*(\mathcal G\otimes K_Y^\vee)[1].
\]
Applying $\mathbf R\pi_{\mathcal M*}\mathbf R\mathcal Hom(-,\mathcal E)$,
and using adjunction and Serre duality on the $3$-fold $Y$, gives a self-dual
triangle
\[
\mathbf R\pi_{\mathcal M*}
\mathbf R\mathcal Hom(\mathcal E,\mathcal E)
\longrightarrow
\mathcal V
\longrightarrow
\mathcal V^\vee[-3].
\]
Consequently,
\[
K_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}
\cong
\det\mathcal V\otimes(\det\mathcal V)^\vee
\cong
\mathcal O_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}.
\]
Since the
triangle is self-dual, it is compatible with $Q_{\mathcal M_X^{\rm cs}}$ and
hence defines the asserted canonical orientation.

For the topological statement, let $\alpha$ be the universal compactly
supported $K$-theory class on $\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}\times X$. The Thom
isomorphism and Bott periodicity, in the notation of
Subsection~\ref{sec:push}, allow us to write
\(
\alpha=\operatorname{Th}^{KU}_{K_Y}(\beta)
\)
for a universal class $\beta$ on $\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}\times Y$; when
$Y$ is non-compact, compactly supported $K$-theory is understood. Put
\[
\mathcal V^{\rm top}
=\pi_{Y!}^{KU,\mathbb C}(\beta^\vee\otimes\beta).
\]
If $u^{KU}_{K_Y}$ is the Thom class, then
\[
(u^{KU}_{K_Y})^\vee u^{KU}_{K_Y}
=u^{KU}_{K_Y}(1-K_Y).
\]
The projection formula and topological Serre duality from
Subsection~\ref{sec:serre-duality-without-quasi-projectivity} therefore give
\[
\pi_{X!}^{KU,\mathbb C}(\alpha^\vee\otimes\alpha)
\simeq
\mathcal V^{\rm top}\oplus(\mathcal V^{\rm top})^\vee.
\]
Taking determinants yields the canonical trivialization
\[
K_{\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}}
\cong
\det\mathcal V^{\rm top}
\otimes(\det\mathcal V^{\rm top})^\vee
\cong
\underline{\mathbb C}_{\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}},
\]
which is compatible with $Q_{\mathcal C_{X,0}^{\rm cs}}$.
For the spin structure determined by the Calabi--Yau structure,
\eqref{complex-spin-pushforward} gives
$\pi_{X!}^{KU,\mathbb C}=\pi_{X!}^{KU,\mathrm{spin}}$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{canonicalThomfunctor}
Define the ``\emph{Thom functor}''
\begin{equation}\label{canonical-bundle-Thom-functor}
\mathcal T_K:
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{U}}_6(\mathbb K)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Bord}^{\operatorname{Spin}}_8(BU,*).
\end{equation}
For an object $[N,f]$, write $[f]\in K^0(N)$ for the class represented by
$f$, and set
\begin{equation}\label{canonical-bundle-Thom-on-objects}
\mathcal T_K[N,f]
:=
\left[
D(K_N),
\operatorname{Th}^{KU}_{K_N}([f])
\right].
\end{equation}

Now let
\[
[W,h]:[N_0,f_0]\longrightarrow[N_1,f_1]
\]
be a morphism. The product form of the stable complex structure near the
boundary gives canonical identifications
\begin{equation}\label{canonical-bundle-boundary-identification}
K_W|_{N_i}\cong K_{N_i},
\qquad i=0,1.
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{canonical-bundle-Thom-on-morphisms}
\mathcal T_K[W,h]
:=
\left[
D(K_W),
\operatorname{Th}^{KU}_{K_W}([h])
\right].
\end{equation}
Here $S(K_W)$ is the relative boundary face and is mapped to the basepoint of
$BU$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{canonical-bundle-Thom-functoriality}
The construction of Definition~\ref{canonicalThomfunctor} gives a symmetric
monoidal functor. It is independent, up to a canonical monoidal natural
isomorphism, of any choices.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
There is a natural stable isomorphism
\[
T^{\mathrm{st},\mathbb C}D(K_N)
\cong
\pi_N^*\bigl(T_N^{\mathrm{st},\mathbb C}\oplus K_N\bigr),
\]
and
\[
\det_{\mathbb C}
\bigl(T_N^{\mathrm{st},\mathbb C}\oplus K_N\bigr)
\cong
\det_{\mathbb C}\bigl(T_N^{\mathrm{st},\mathbb C}\bigr)
\otimes K_N
\cong
\underline{\mathbb C}.
\]
Thus $D(K_N)$ carries a canonical stable $SU$-structure, and hence a
canonical spin structure. The same statement for a bordism $W$ is compatible
with the boundary identifications
\eqref{canonical-bundle-boundary-identification}. Moreover, the Thom complex
is acyclic on $S(K_W)$, so \eqref{canonical-bundle-Thom-on-morphisms} is a
relative spin bordism over $(BU,*)$.

For this spin structure, the two pushforwards in complex $K$-theory agree by
\eqref{complex-spin-pushforward}.

The Thom classes are natural under restriction and gluing, and multiplicative
under disjoint union. Hence \eqref{canonical-bundle-Thom-on-objects} and
\eqref{canonical-bundle-Thom-on-morphisms} define a symmetric monoidal
functor. 

The rest is clear.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{local-fourfold-orientation-comparison}
First of all,
\begin{equation}\label{local-fourfold-topological-conditions}
\left\langle
 \bar\alpha\smile\operatorname{Sq}_\partial^2(\bar\alpha),
 [Z_N,\partial Z_N]
\right\rangle=0
\quad\text{for every }\alpha\in H^3(Z_N,\partial Z_N;\mathbb Z).
\end{equation}

Suppose also that for a $K$-theory class $\xi_f$ on $(Z_N, \partial Z_N)$
\begin{equation}
\\[3pt]
\kappa(\xi_f)
=c_2(\xi_f)-c_1(\xi_f)^2
=0
\quad\text{in }H^4(Z_N,\partial Z_N;\mathbb Z).
\end{equation}
Then, on the component represented by $\xi_f$, the two $2$-morphisms
coincide:
\[
\omega_{\rm Shi}|_{\xi_f}=\omega_{\rm JU}|_{\xi_f}.
\]
These equalities are compatible with complex bordisms and disjoint unions
whenever all the components involved satisfy
\eqref{local-fourfold-topological-conditions}.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{local-curve-orientation-comparison}
Let $C$ be a compact Riemann surface, and let $E\to C$ be a rank-$3$ complex
vector bundle such that
\[
c_1(TC)+c_1(E)=0
\quad\text{in }H^2(C;\mathbb Z).
\]
Then Shi's orientation and the Joyce--Upmeier orientation on
$X = \operatorname{Tot}_C(E)$ canonically coincide.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
First of all, note that Shi's orientation $\omega_{Shi}$ can be restricted to $\omega_{Shi}^r$ on $$\operatorname{Maps}_{cs}(X, BSU \times \mathbb Z)$$ via the map $$f: \operatorname{Maps}_{cs}(X, BSU \times \mathbb Z) \to \operatorname{Maps}_{cs}(X, BU \times \mathbb Z)$$ induced by $E \mapsto E \oplus \Lambda^{top} E^*$.

Since Shi's orientation has an explicit, purely algebraic definition via topological Serre duality and Thom classes, a (not entirely pleasant but explicit) calculation shows that $f^*\omega_{Shi}^r = \omega_{Shi}$.

Thus, it is enough to prove that $\omega_{Shi}^r$ coincides with the  Joyce-Upmeier's orientation defined earlier on $\operatorname{Maps}_{cs}(X, BSU \times \mathbb Z)$ (before the pull-back to $\operatorname{Maps}_{cs}(X, BU \times \mathbb Z)$). 

For this, note that the space $\operatorname{Tot}_C(E)$ admits a spin-embedding into $\mathcal S^6 \times \mathbb C^2$. Thus, the statement follows from the results of Section \ref{S6C2} by excision.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
From our discussion of the relation between $6$ and $8$-dimensional bordism categories, it should by now be clear that the ratio of Shi's and Joyce-Upmeier's orientations on the local $CY4$s gives a morphism 

$$\tilde{\Omega}_6^U(BSU) \to \mathbb Z_2$$

where $\Omega_6^U(BSU)$ is the $6$-th almost complex bordism group of $BSU$, and that it is enough to prove that this morphism vanishes.

An elementary computation with Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence gives

$$\tilde{\Omega}_6^U(BSU)= \{(a, b) \ | \ a-b \in 2\mathbb Z\} \simeq \mathbb Z^2.$$

An explicit basis can be provided as follows.

Consider $N = \mathbb P^2  \times \mathbb P^1$, $L = \operatorname{pr}_1^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)$, $M = \operatorname{pr}_2^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$.

It is easy to see that the classes $(L-1)^2$ and $(L-1)(M-1)$ form the basis of $\tilde{\Omega}_6^U(BSU)$. Since both of these classes have representatives supported on local curves, theorem now follows from the proposition.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{local-curve-representations}
Let $z=kx$ and $u=kb$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-representation-classes}
M_z=-8z,\qquad
A_{2u}=r(8z),\qquad S_{2u}=r(-8z),\qquad
p_*\alpha_U(z)=2\alpha_K.
\end{equation}
Here $A_v$ and $S_v$ are the reduced real classes obtained from the adjoint
and half spin representations of $K$, respectively,
$p:E_8/U\to E_8/K$, and $\alpha_K\in\pi_8(E_8/K)$ has boundary $u$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Let $W$ be the standard complex representation of $\operatorname{SU}(8)$.
The adjoint and half spin representations give
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-E8-branching}
\left.\mathfrak e_8\right|_{\operatorname{SU}(8)}
\cong\mathfrak u(8)\oplus(\Lambda^2W)_{\mathbb R}
 \oplus(W\oplus\Lambda^3W)_{\mathbb R}.
\end{equation}
See \cite[Chapters~6--7]{AdamsExceptional} for the subgroup
$\operatorname{HSpin}(16)\subset E_8$, and
\cite[Section~20.1]{FultonHarris} for the exterior power description of the spin
representations.  With our convention, the complex representation underlying
$\mathfrak m$ is
$W\oplus\Lambda^3W\oplus(\Lambda^2W)^\vee$.

Put $q=8+z$.  Note that
$\psi^2z=16z$ and $\psi^3z=81z$.  The Newton identities therefore give
$\lambda^2q-28=0$ and $\lambda^3q-56=-9z$.  It follows from
\eqref{local-curve-E8-branching} that
$M_z=z-9z+0=-8z$.  The quotient
$\mathfrak{so}(16)/\mathfrak u(8)$ is the underlying real representation of
$\Lambda^2W$.

Applying the Newton identity in $\widetilde{KO}^0(S^8)$ gives $A_u=8u$.
Since the sum of the adjoint and half spin representations is the restriction
of the adjoint representation
of $E_8$, and the induced $E_8$ bundle on $S^8$ is trivial, one has
$S_u=-8u$.  As $r(z)=2u$, the middle two identities in
\eqref{local-curve-representation-classes} follow.  Finally, the boundary
maps for $U\to E_8\to E_8/U$ and $K\to E_8\to E_8/K$ are isomorphisms in
the relevant degrees. It is now clear that
$p_*\alpha_U(z)=2\alpha_K$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{local-curve-theta}
The quadratic map $\operatorname{Ad}$ and the convention of
Remark~\ref{orientation-conventions} determine an isomorphism
\[
\theta_z:O_{\operatorname{Ad}}(z)\longrightarrow
O_U(z)\otimes O_M(z).
\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Distributivity for the quadratic map $\operatorname{Ad}$, followed
by the real identification induced by a Hermitian metric on $V_z$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-adjoint-homotopy}
\begin{split}
h_z:\operatorname{Ad}(z)
&\simeq
 A_U(z)\oplus r(-8z^\vee)\\
&\xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{id}\oplus d_z\ }
 A_U(z)\oplus r(-8z).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Here $d_z:r(-8z^\vee)\to r(-8z)$ is the real identification induced by the
Hermitian metric on $V_z$.  The real determinant of complex conjugation on
$\mathbb C^n$ is $(-1)^n$.
Applying this to the kernel and cokernel, the isomorphism of orientation
torsors induced by $d_z$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-duality-sign}
(d_z)_*o_{\mathbb C}(-8z^\vee)
=(-1)^{\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}(-8z)}o_{\mathbb C}(-8z)
=o_{\mathbb C}(-8z),
\end{equation}
since $\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}(-8z)=-8k$.  Thus $d_z$ preserves the
complex orientation.

Applying the orientation functor to $h_z$ gives
$\theta_z^0:O_{\operatorname{Ad}}(z)\to
O_U(z)\otimes O(-8z)$.  By
Lemma~\ref{local-curve-representations}, $M_z=-8z$.  Since
$\pi_1\operatorname{Map}_*(S^8,BU)=0$, this equality determines an
isomorphism
\[
\rho_z:O(-8z)\longrightarrow O_M(z),\qquad
\rho_z(o_{\mathbb C}(-8z))=o_{\mathbb C}(M_z).
\]
We set
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-theta-definition}
\theta_z=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\rho_z)\circ\theta_z^0:
O_{\operatorname{Ad}}(z)\longrightarrow
O_U(z)\otimes O_M(z).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{local-curve-JU-characterization}
The Joyce--Upmeier orientation is characterized by
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-JU-value}
(\Phi_{\alpha_U(z)}\circ\theta_z)(o_{\rm JU}(z))=+1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Pull $\lambda_{8,8}^{\operatorname{SU},{\rm c}}$ back to the bordism
category associated to $S^8$.  The class $c_2(P_z)$ maps to zero in
$H^4(S^8;\mathbb Z)$.  The cohomology orientation torsor at zero has its
canonical trivialization.  Via
$\lambda_{8,8}^{\operatorname{SU},{\rm c}}$ and the identifications above,
let $o_{{\rm JU},U}(z)\in O_U(z)$ be the element corresponding to $+1$.
The morphism defined by $\alpha_U(z)$ also maps to the identity
morphism of the zero object, since $H^3(S^8;\mathbb Z)=0$.
Naturality of $\lambda_{8,8}^{\operatorname{SU},{\rm c}}$ therefore gives
\[
\Phi_{\alpha_U(z)}
\bigl(o_{{\rm JU},U}(z)\otimes o_{\mathbb C}(M_z)\bigr)=+1.
\]

It is eady to see that
$\theta_z(o_{\rm JU}(z))=
o_{{\rm JU},U}(z)\otimes o_{\mathbb C}(M_z)$, which proves
\eqref{local-curve-JU-value}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{local-curve-ABS-comparison}
There is a based homotopy $H_{\rm rc}$ in $\operatorname{Spin}(16)$ which
realizes $r(c(kb))=2kb$. If $H$ is any based lift of a homotopy realizing
$p_*\alpha_U(z)=2\alpha_K$, then, after applying either the adjoint or the
half spin representation, $H$ and $H_{\rm rc}$ induce the same isomorphism
of orientation torsors.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The stabilization map
$\pi_7(\operatorname{SO}(8))\to\pi_7(\operatorname{SO})$ is surjective.
Choose a based oriented real vector bundle $B_k\to S^8$ of rank $8$ such
that $[B_k]-8=kb$, and let
$g_k:S^7\to\operatorname{Spin}(8)$ be a lift of its clutching map. Since
$[V_z]-8=c([B_k]-8)$ and $\pi_7(\operatorname{U}(8))$ is stable, we may
choose a based isomorphism of $\operatorname{SU}(8)$ bundles
$V_z\cong B_k\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$.

The real isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-ABS-realification}
(B_k\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C)_{\mathbb R}
 \longrightarrow B_k\oplus B_k,
\qquad v+\mathrm i w\longmapsto(v,w),
\end{equation}
has sign $(-1)^{8\cdot7/2}=+1$ relative to the complex orientation on the
source and the product orientation on the target. It is therefore
orientation preserving. Since
$H^2(S^8;\mathbb Z_2)=H^1(S^8;\mathbb Z_2)=0$, the spin structures on the
two sides exist and are unique. The isomorphism has a unique spin lift after
its value at the basepoint is fixed. Using the standard homomorphism
$\operatorname{Spin}(8)\times\operatorname{Spin}(8)
\to\operatorname{Spin}(16)$, it gives a based homotopy
\[
H_{\rm rc}:\widehat f_k\simeq g_k\oplus g_k
\]
in $\operatorname{Spin}(16)$, where $\widehat f_k$ is the spin clutching
map of the underlying real bundle of $V_z$.

Choose the representative of $2\alpha_K$ whose boundary is represented by
$g_k\oplus g_k$. The equality $p_*\alpha_U(z)=2\alpha_K$ gives a based
homotopy between the images of the two endpoints in
$K=\operatorname{HSpin}(16)$. Once its initial lift is fixed, it lifts
uniquely to a homotopy $H$ in $\operatorname{Spin}(16)$.

The difference between $H$ and $H_{\rm rc}$ is a class
$\tau\in\pi_8\operatorname{Spin}(16)\cong\mathbb Z_2$. These homotopy
groups are stable in degrees $7$ and $8$. A generator of
$\pi_8(\operatorname{SO})$ is obtained by composing a generator of
$\pi_7(\operatorname{SO})$ with the stable Hopf element. By
\eqref{local-curve-representation-classes}, the adjoint and half spin
representations act on $\pi_7(\operatorname{SO})$ by multiplication by
$8$ and $-8$, respectively. They therefore act trivially on
$\pi_8(\operatorname{SO})\cong\mathbb Z_2$; see \cite{BottStable}.
Consequently the two homotopies become homotopic relative to their
endpoints after either representation is applied, and hence induce the same
isomorphism of orientation torsors.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{local-curve-complex-orientations}
As we have already said only too often, for a real bundle $E$, there is a natural real isomorphism
\[
(E\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C)_{\mathbb R}
 \longrightarrow E\oplus E,\qquad
v+\mathrm iw\longmapsto(v,w),
\]
with the two summands in the displayed order.  It extends by
stabilization to virtual bundles.


When we refer below to the complex orientations of $A_{2u}$ and
$S_{2u}$, we, thus, mean ones coming from identifications $A_{2u} = r(c(A_u))$, $S_{2u} = r(c(S_u))$.

Finally, let us note that, if $D$ is a real Fredholm operator of index $n$, the product
orientation for $D\oplus D$ differs from the complex orientation of
$D\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ by
$(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$ under the natural comparison isomorphism.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{local-curve-Thom-comparison}
There is an isomorphism
$\chi_z:O(8z)\to O_U(z)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-complex-value}
\Phi_{\alpha_U(z)}
\bigl(\chi_z(o_{\mathbb C}(8z))\otimes o_{\mathbb C}(M_z)\bigr)=+1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
\textit{Step 1.}
We compute the value of $\Phi_{2\alpha_K}$ on the complex orientations.
Write $O_A(u)=O(A_u)$ and $O_S(u)=O(S_u)$ for the orientation torsors of
$A_u,S_u$, and let
$\Phi_{\alpha_K}:O_A(u)\otimes O_S(u)\to\{\pm1\}$ be the
isomorphism induced by $\alpha_K$.  Choose elements $o_A,o_S$ and write
$\Phi_{\alpha_K}(o_A\otimes o_S)=\delta$, where
$\delta\in\{\pm1\}$.  Put $a=8k$ and $s=-8k$.

Representing $2\alpha_K$ by two copies of $\alpha_K$ in disjoint balls
defines an isomorphism
$\Phi_{2\alpha_K}:O_A(2u)\otimes O_S(2u)\to\{\pm1\}$.  The
symmetric monoidal structure then immediately shows that its value on the complex orientations (that is, orientations $o_{\mathbb C}$)  determined by
$A_{2u}=r(8z)$ and $S_{2u}=r(-8z)$ is
$+1.$

\textit{Step 2.}
We pass from $K$ to $U$.  By Lemma~\ref{local-curve-representations},
$p_*\alpha_U(z)=2\alpha_K$.  The quotient representations restrict to
\[
\mathfrak{so}(16)/\mathfrak u(8)\cong(\Lambda^2W)_{\mathbb R},
\qquad
\mathfrak e_8/\mathfrak{so}(16)
\cong(W\oplus\Lambda^3W)_{\mathbb R}.
\]


\textit{Step 3.}
Apply the adjoint and half spin
representations to $H_{\rm rc}$.  With the convention of Step~2, the
resulting isomorphisms are
\[
T_A:O_U(z)\longrightarrow O(8z),\qquad
T_S:O_M(z)\longrightarrow O(-8z).
\]
Lemma~\ref{local-curve-ABS-comparison} shows that the same isomorphisms are
obtained from any based lift which realizes
$p_*\alpha_U(z)=2\alpha_K$.

Naturality gives
\begin{equation}\label{local-curve-Phi-comparison}
\Phi_{\alpha_U(z)}
=\Phi_{2\alpha_K}\circ(T_A\otimes T_S).
\end{equation}
The rest is clear.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{local-curve-Koszul-comparison}
Let $u_{\underline{\mathbb C}}^{KU}$ be the Thom class of the trivial
complex line over $S^6$. The Koszul complex and the fixed trivialization of
